The builders of the Empire State Building faced many obstacles in attempting to allow dirigibles, also known as blimps, to dock there.
One of the biggest obstacles was safety.
Most dirigibles from outside of the United States used hydrogen rather than helium, and hydrogen is highly flammable.
If a dirigible caught on fire above a densely populated area like downtown New York, it could be a disaster.
Another challenge was the constantly shifting winds on top of the building.
Even if the dirigible were tethered to the mooring mast, the back of the ship would swivel around and around the mast.

Dirigibles moored in open landing fields could be weighted down in the back with lead weights, but using these at the Empire State Building, where they would be dangling high above pedestrians on the street, was neither practical nor safe.
In addition, there was an existing law against airships flying too low over urban areas, making it illegal for a ship to even approach the area.
These challenges led to the idea of using the mooring mast for dirigibles being abandoned.
They couldn't just drop the mooring mast on top of the building or it would be unstable.
But most importantly since the winds kept changing it would never stay still.
The problem of foreign blimps using hydrogen rather than helium made it to dangerouse to the public.

Dear Editor,  As a student in junior high school, I strongly believe that censorship in libraries is not the solution to protect children from inappropriate materials.
While it is true that some materials, such as books, music, movies, and magazines, may contain content that is offensive to some people, removing them from the shelves is not the answer.
Katherine Paterson, an author, once said, "'All of us can think of a book that we hope none of our children or any other children have taken off the shelf.
But if I have the right to remove that book from the shelf -- that work I abhor -- then you also have exactly the same right and so does everyone else.
And then we have no books left on the shelf for any of us'."
This quote perfectly captures the essence of why censorship is not the solution to protect children from inappropriate materials in libraries.
I do agree that not all books are appropriate for little kids to be reading.
I also think that the kids of today know more than what I knew at that age.
However, I believe that it is up to the parents or guardians to monitor what their children read, watch, or listen to.
Libraries should not be responsible for making those decisions for families.
It is important for children to have the freedom to explore different genres of literature and to develop their own opinions and beliefs.
Furthermore, censorship in libraries can also limit the availability of important and educational materials.
For example, books on controversial topics such as race, gender, and sexuality can provide valuable insights and perspectives for readers.
Removing these books from the shelves can hinder intellectual growth and critical thinking skills.
By limiting children on what movies and magazines they can get from a library is just enough to protect their eyes from what is necessary.
I beleive that everyone should have an equal freedom to read whichever book they might pick off of the shelf

The builders of the Empire State Building attempted to create a mast where dirigibles could dock.
However, they faced several obstacles in making this happen.
Firstly, a thousand-foot dirigible moored at the top of the building, held by a single cable tether, would add stress to the building’s frame.
The stress of the dirigible’s load and the wind pressure would have to be transmitted all the way to the building’s foundation, which was nearly eleven hundred feet below.
Over sixty thousand dollars’ worth of modifications had to be made to the building’s framework.
Secondly, hydrogen was used in most dirigibles from outside of the United States, and hydrogen is highly flammable.
This was an issue because hydrogen is very flammable and if it were to catch on fire in New York, thousands of people would be hurt/killed.
The greatest obstacle was the wind.
The winds on top of the building were constantly shifting due to violent air currents.
Even if the dirigible were tethered to the mooring mast, the back of the ship would swivel around and around the mooring mast.

Dirigibles moored in open landing fields could be weighted down in the back with lead weights, but using these at the Empire State Building, where they would be dangling high above pedestrians on the street, was neither practical nor safe.
The other practical reason why dirigibles could not moor at the Empire State Building was an existing law against airships flying too low over urban areas.
This law would make it illegal for a ship to ever tie up to the building or even approach the area.
Two dirigibles did attempt to reach the building before the entire idea was dropped.
The U.S. Navy dirigible Los Angeles approached the mooring mast but could not get close enough to tie up because of forceful winds.

Fearing that the wind would blow the dirigible onto the sharp spires of other buildings in the area, which would puncture the dirigible’s shell, the captain could not even take his hands off the control levers.
The author ended the story with this paragraph because it sums up the story.
During the story, Saeng was testing herself on whether or not love her new country.
She failed her driver's test and felt homesick when she saw the hibiscus plant because it reminded her of home.

?Her mother is referring to her family and how they can adapt like the flower did.
If Saeng can stop thinking of how the flower at home is more beautiful and start thinking how the hibiscus here is stronger, she will pass the test she has given to herself.
When the flower blooms again, she will do that.
The author finishes the story with this paragraph because it sums up the story by letting the reader make an inference, and by giving them a hint of what will happen next.

Even if the dirigible were tethered to the mooring mast, the back of the ship would swivel around and around the mooring mast.

Another obstacle was an existing law against airships flying too low over urban areas.
This law stated that airships couldn't fly too low over urban areas making it illegal for ships to ever tie up to the building or even go near the area.
The mooring equipment was never completely installed causing the idea of using the mooring mast for dirigibles to slowly disappear.

Instead, we should encourage open-mindedness and tolerance.

As a junior high school student, I believe that censorship in libraries is a complicated issue.
On one hand, I understand why some people may want certain materials, such as books, music, movies, and magazines, removed from the shelves if they are found offensive.
However, I do not believe that censorship is the answer.
Katherine Paterson, the author of "Bridge to Terabithia," once said, "'All of us can think of a book that we hope none of our children or any other children have taken off the shelf.
But if I have the right to remove that book from the shelf -- that work I abhor -- then you also have exactly the same right and so does everyone else.
And then we have no books left on the shelf for any of us'."
This quote perfectly sums up my opinion on censorship in libraries.
Then again, this library had an upstairs that the more 'colorful' books were at.

The Empire State building faced hardships while trying to dock their dirigibles.
The biggest problem was the safety concern as most of the dirigibles outside of the United States used hydrogen, which is highly flammable.

The German dirigible Hindenburg was destroyed by fire in Lakehurst, New Jersey, on May 6, 1937, and the owners of the Empire State Building realized how much worse the accident could have been if it had taken place above a densely populated area such as downtown New York.
Another problem was the shifting winds on top of the building due to violent air currents.
Even if the dirigible was tethered to the mooring mast, the back of the ship would swivel around and around the mooring mast.

Dirigibles moored in open landing fields could be weighted down in the back with lead weights, but using these at the Empire State Building, where they would be dangling high above pedestrians on the street, was neither practical nor safe.
There was also an existing law against airships flying too low over urban areas, which would make it illegal for a ship to ever tie up to the building or even approach the area.
Two dirigibles attempted to reach the building before the entire idea was dropped, but they could not get close enough to tie up because of forceful winds.
In the late 1930s, dirigibles were replaced by airplanes and the idea of using the mooring mast for dirigibles and their passengers had quietly disappeared.

I am writing a persuasive essay to a newspaper reflecting my views on censorship.
I think if a book has so much censorship in it that it then needs to be put in a section where only people at the right age should be able to view it.
I believe that censorship is a complicated issue that affects everyone, especially in libraries.
Some people argue that certain materials, such as books, music, movies, magazines, etc., should be removed from the shelves if they are found offensive.
However, I think that censorship in libraries is unnecessary and can even be harmful.
Firstly, censorship infringes on our freedom of speech and the right to access information.
It is important that we have the freedom to express ourselves and access different viewpoints, even if they are controversial or unpopular.
By censoring certain materials, we limit our ability to learn and grow as individuals.
It is also important to note that what one person finds offensive may not be offensive to another.
Therefore, it is not fair to impose our beliefs on others and limit their access to information.
Secondly, censorship can be harmful to young people.
By limiting their access to certain materials, we are sheltering them from the realities of the world.
This can lead to a lack of understanding and empathy for others who may have different experiences or beliefs.
It is important that young people are exposed to different viewpoints and ideas, so they can form their own opinions and become well-rounded individuals.
Lastly, censorship can lead to a slippery slope.
If we start censoring certain materials, where do we draw the line?
Who decides what is offensive and what is not?
If we start censoring books, what is stopping us from censoring other forms of media?
Allowing censorship in libraries opens the door for more extreme forms of censorship, which can lead to a society where free speech is no longer valued or protected.
In conclusion, censorship in libraries is unnecessary and can even be harmful.
It is important that we have the freedom to access information and different viewpoints, even if they are controversial or unpopular.
By limiting our access to certain materials, we limit our ability to learn and grow as individuals.
It is important that we trust individuals to make their own decisions about what they want to read, watch, or listen to.

In the memoir "Home: The Blueprints of Our Lives" written by Narciso Rodriguez, the author creates a mood of warmth, love, and gratitude.
He describes his childhood home in the Ironbound section of Newark, New Jersey, as a simple house where his parents created a traditional Cuban home.
The heart of the home was the kitchen, where his parents shared cooking duties and instilled in him a love of cooking.
The innocence of childhood, the congregation of family and friends, and endless celebrations formed the backdrop to life in their warm home.

Despite living in a neighborhood made up of mostly Spanish, Cuban, and Italian immigrants at a time when overt racism was the norm, Rodriguez's parents kept their arms and their door open to people who were clearly in need.

Many people, including their landlord's daughter Alegria, surrogate grandparents Sergio and Edelmira, aunts, cousins, and countless extended family members came and went, and there was often someone staying with them temporarily until they were able to get back on their feet.
Rodriguez's parents had come to this country with courage, without any knowledge of the language or the culture, to give their children a better life.
They struggled both personally and financially, but their faith that this struggle would lead them and their children to better times drove them to endure these hard times.
Rodriguez is grateful to his parents for their love and sacrifice, and he will never forget the lessons they taught him about the importance of family and friends.
In conclusion, Rodriguez's memoir creates a mood of warmth, love, and gratitude as he describes his childhood home and the close-knit community in which he grew up.

The highest open observation deck, intended for disembarking passengers, has never been open to the public.
The final problem was that there was a law forbidding aircraft to be a certain distance from a city.

Builders of the Empire State Building were faced with obstacles created by both nature and government law.
One safety threat to the city was that international dirigibles most commonly carried hydrogen rather than helium.
As shown through the German dirigible Hindenburg, hydrogen is highly flammable.
Imagine the catastrophe that would take place if a dirigible were to go up in flames in New York City.
Another obstacle builders faced were the high winds on top of the building constantly shifting because of ""violent air currents.""
The powerful winds would cause the back of the ship to swivel around and around the mast.
Usually lead weights would anchor the back in place, but the dangling bags of lead would pose a threat to the citizens below.
With the ferocious winds around, pilots would have to skillfully maneuver around sharp spires of the buildings.
Additionally, there was an existing law against airships flying too low over urban areas, which made it illegal for a ship to ever tie up to the building or even approach the area.
Two dirigibles attempted to reach the building before the entire idea was dropped.
The U.S. Navy dirigible Los Angeles approached the mooring mast but could not get close enough to tie up because of forceful winds.

Fearing that the wind would blow the dirigible onto the sharp spires of other buildings in the area, which would puncture the dirigible's shell, the captain could not even take his hands off the control levers.
Another dirigible, the Goodyear blimp Columbia, attempted a publicity stunt where it would tie up and deliver a bundle of newspapers to the Empire State Building.
Because the complete dirigible mooring equipment had never been installed, a worker atop the mooring mast would have to catch the bundle of papers on a rope dangling from the blimp.
The papers were delivered in this fashion, but after this stunt, the idea of using the mooring mast was shelved.

Constructing a building such as the Empire State requires a lot of careful planning, as well as having to face the copious obstacles thrown at the builders' way.
One such obstacle was the idea of having a mooring mast at the top of the building for dirigibles to dock.
This was a dream of the aviation pioneers who believed that dirigibles would become the transportation of the future.
However, the builders faced many challenges in attempting to allow dirigibles to dock there.
Allowing a gargantuan blimp to dock at the top of the Empire State would "add stress to the building's frame" from the blimp's weight.
The stress of the dirigible’s load and the wind pressure would have to be transmitted all the way to the building’s foundation, which was nearly eleven hundred feet below.
Over sixty thousand dollars’ worth of modifications had to be made to the building’s framework.
Additionally, most dirigibles used hydrogen that is highly flammable, which could have caused a dangerous situation if a dirigible caught fire.
The winds on top of the building were constantly shifting due to violent air currents, making it difficult for dirigibles to stay in one place.
Even if the dirigible were tethered to the mooring mast, the back of the ship would swivel around and around the mooring mast.

Dirigibles moored in open landing fields could be weighted down in the back with lead weights, but using these at the Empire State Building, where they would be dangling high above pedestrians on the street, was neither practical nor safe.
Finally, the existing law against airships flying too low over urban areas would make it illegal for a ship to ever tie up to the building or even approach the area.
The builders of the Empire State Building faced many challenges in attempting to allow dirigibles to dock there, and ultimately the idea was abandoned due to safety concerns and practical challenges.

The builders of the Empire State Building faced many obstacles in attempting to allow dirigibles to dock there.
Dirigibles are very long, and the previous structure would not be enough to support it with the high blowing winds.
Safety was also an issue with adding the mooring mast.
Blimps from outside the United States were filled with hydrogen, which is extremely flammable, instead of helium.
This was a major concern, especially after the Hindenburg disaster in 1937.
Additionally, the winds on top of the building were constantly shifting due to violent air currents.
Even if the dirigible were tethered to the mooring mast, the back of the ship would swivel around and around the mooring mast.

Dirigibles moored in open landing fields could be weighted down in the back with lead weights, but using these at the Empire State Building, where they would be dangling high above pedestrians on the street, was neither practical nor safe.
Another obstacle was an existing law against airships flying too low over urban areas, making it illegal for a ship to ever tie up to the building or even approach the area.

Economists view this data as a promising sign for the overall health of the economy as it navigates through ongoing challenges.
The job market's resilience bodes well for continued economic growth in the coming months.

The architects had to modify and strengthen the steel frame of the Empire State Building to accommodate the mooring mast.
The dirigible’s load and wind pressure would have to be transmitted all the way to the building’s foundation, which was nearly eleven hundred feet below.
Over sixty thousand dollars’ worth of modifications had to be made to the building’s framework.
The architects designed a shiny glass and chrome-nickel stainless steel tower that would be illuminated from inside, with a stepped-back design that imitated the overall shape of the building itself.
The rocket-shaped mast would have four wings at its corners, of shiny aluminum, and would rise to a conical roof that would house the mooring arm.
The winds on top of the building were constantly shifting due to violent air currents.
Even if the dirigible were tethered to the mooring mast, the back of the ship would swivel around and around the mooring mast.

This law would make it illegal for a ship to ever tie up to the building or even approach the area, although two dirigibles did attempt to reach the building before the entire idea was dropped.
Lead weights, the only solution to this, would disrupt pedestrians.

BANGKOK (AP) — A Thai court of appeals has dismissed criminal defamation charges against a British labor rights activist who was sued by a fruit packaging company after he alleged human rights violations at its factory.
Andy Hall's protracted legal battle stemmed from a 2013 report he researched for Finnish consumer organization Finnwatch that alleged labor abuses at Natural Fruit's pineapple canning operation.
The court ruled that Hall's findings were based on legitimate research and fell within the boundaries of freedom of expression and the right to information.
This decision marks a significant victory for human rights advocates and activists who face legal threats for exposing labor abuses in Thailand's industrial sector.
Hall expressed relief at the court's decision, emphasizing the importance of protecting whistleblowers and ensuring transparency in supply chains.
The dismissal of the case is seen as a positive development in the ongoing efforts to uphold labor rights and combat exploitation in the region.

The builders of the Empire State Building faced many obstacles in attempting to allow dirigibles to dock there.
One of the biggest obstacles was the stress that a thousand-foot dirigible would add to the building's frame.
This stress would have to be transmitted all the way to the building's foundation, which was nearly eleven hundred feet below.
The designers had to make over sixty thousand dollars worth of modifications to the building's framework to account for the pressure.
Also, the winds on top of the building were constantly shifting due to violent air currents, which made it difficult for dirigibles to stay tethered to the mooring mast.
The back of the ship would swivel around and around the mooring mast, which was not safe for pedestrians on the street.
Additionally, there was an existing law against airships flying too low over urban areas.
This meant that the dirigibles would not be allowed to even get close to the building, let alone dock on it.
Eventually, these obstacles and other safety issues, such as hydrogen inside, the blimp being highly flammable, caused the idea to dissappear.

The hot and dry desert terrain made it difficult for the cyclist to find water, causing him to become dehydrated and tired.

The cyclist had to pump water from a rusty pump and drink water that tasted like battery acid.
He also had to suck on stones to keep his mind off his thirst.
The lack of water and the heat caused the cyclist to become delirious and think he was going to die.

This essay is to describe my opinion on if certain materials that can be offensive, should be removed from shelves in libraries.

If there is something that is not suitable for people of all ages, then it should not be in a library.
In addition, libraries can be held responsible for what they have on their shelves.
If someone is offended by something in a library, they can sue the library.
So if they just take any books, music, magazines, or movies that are not suitable for people of all ages, they can cut the risk of being sued.
Libraries are meant to provide information anyways.
They have no need for things that are offensive, because rarely something that is offensive, provides information.
Libraries should just contain what they were made for: encyclopedias, dictionaries, books, and other books that can provide useful information to people.

As a student and a frequent visitor to my local library, I strongly believe that censorship in libraries should not be enforced.
Censorship is defined as the suppression or prohibition of any parts of books, films, news, etc.
that are considered obscene, politically unacceptable, or a threat to security.
However, I believe that censorship is not the solution to eliminating the problem of offensive materials in libraries.
Firstly, censorship goes against the First Amendment of the United States Constitution, which guarantees freedom of speech and expression for all citizens.
By censoring materials in libraries, we are limiting the freedom of expression of authors and artists who create these materials.
Everyone has the right to express themselves and share their ideas with others, even if some may find it offensive.
It is up to the individual to decide whether or not they want to engage with that material.
Secondly, censorship is subjective and can vary from person to person.
What one person might find offensive, another might find valuable and informative.
By censoring materials, we are limiting the opportunity for individuals to learn and gain knowledge about different perspectives and ideas.
It is important to have a diverse range of materials available in libraries to cater to the interests and needs of all individuals.
Moreover, censorship does not solve the problem of offensive materials in libraries.
It simply hides the problem and does not address the root cause of why these materials are considered offensive in the first place.
It is important to have open and honest discussions about these materials and why they may be considered offensive.
This allows individuals to understand different perspectives and develop their own opinions about the materials.
In conclusion, censorship in libraries should not be enforced.
It goes against the First Amendment, limits the opportunity for individuals to learn and gain knowledge, and does not solve the problem of offensive materials in libraries.
Instead, we should focus on having open and honest discussions about these materials and why they may be considered offensive.
I highly disagree and I think it's a negative outlook on our society by putting those things in our future generation's hands to read.
So by putting censorship in our libraries, not only will calm down some of the problems that are re-occuring in our communities, it just might eliminate the problem completely.

Libraries are known as places where a person can go to find material on almost any topic they could want to learn about, whether that material is a book, movie, or magazine.
Anyone can use the library, and it is a valuable resource to many people.
So why do some libraries insist on removing some of those valuable materials from their shelves?
In past years, censorship in libraries has been the focus of many news reports.
In almost all cases, library patrons have been angry that certain materials have been deemed unsuitable to be offered at the library.
I have to say that I agree with them.
People have a right to choose what books they want to read, what movies they want to watch, and what music they want to listen to.
Censorship in libraries is a big problem.
Some people believe that certain books, movies, or music should be removed from the shelves if they are found offensive.
They say that these materials could be harmful to young people or that they could promote bad behavior.
But I think that everyone has the right to choose what they want to read or watch.
If we start removing books or movies that some people find offensive, where do we draw the line?
What if someone finds a book about a certain religion or political belief offensive?
Should we remove that book too?
Katherine Paterson, the author of many popular books, said it best when she said, "All of us can think of a book that we hope none of our children or any other children have taken off the shelf.
But if I have the right to remove that book from the shelf -- that work I abhor -- then you also have exactly the same right and so does everyone else.
And then we have no books left on the shelf for any of us."
This quote means that if we start removing books that some people find offensive, eventually we won't have any books left on the shelves for anyone to read.
In conclusion, censorship in libraries is a big problem.
People have the right to choose what they want to read or watch, and we shouldn't take that right away from them.
If we start removing books or movies that some people find offensive, eventually we won't have any books left on the shelves for anyone to read.
We need to respect everyone's right to choose what they want to read or watch, and we need to make sure that our libraries are full of diverse materials that can help people learn and grow.

The builders of the Empire State Building faced many obstacles in attempting to allow dirigibles to dock there.
One of the biggest obstacles was safety.
Most dirigibles from outside of the United States used hydrogen, which is highly flammable, instead of helium.

When the German dirigible Hindenburg was destroyed by fire in New Jersey, the owners of the Empire State Building realized how much worse that accident could have been if it had taken place above a densely populated area such as downtown New York.
The winds on top of the building were also constantly shifting due to violent air currents, making it difficult to safely dock a dirigible.
Even if the dirigible were tethered to the mooring mast, the back of the ship would swivel around and around the mooring mast.
Dirigibles moored in open landing fields could be weighted down in the back with lead weights, but using these at the Empire State Building was neither practical nor safe.
Another obstacle was an existing law against airships flying too low over urban areas, which would make it illegal for a ship to ever tie up to the building or even approach the area.
In December 1930, the U.S. Navy dirigible Los Angeles approached the mooring mast but could not get close enough to tie up because of forceful winds.
After all the rigorous work put into the mooring mast was completed, it became clear that it would never be used for its original purpose.

When people wanted to dock the dirigibles on top of the Empire State Building, there were many problems that occur.

One of those problems was that if they wanted to dock on top of the building, then they would have to build a steal frame that had to go all the way down to the foundation of the building which was eleven hundred feet below.
This was because a thousand-foot dirigible moored at the top of the building, held by a single cable tether, would add stress to the building’s frame.
The stress of the dirigible’s load and the wind pressure would have to be transmitted all the way to the building’s foundation.
Over sixty thousand dollars’ worth of modifications had to be made to the building’s framework.
The architects could not simply drop a mooring mast on top of the Empire State Building’s flat roof.

Rather than building a utilitarian mast without any ornamentation, the architects designed a shiny glass and chrome-nickel stainless steel tower that would be illuminated from inside, with a stepped-back design that imitated the overall shape of the building itself.
The rocket-shaped mast would have four wings at its corners, of shiny aluminum, and would rise to a conical roof that would house the mooring arm.

The winches and control machinery for the dirigible mooring would be housed in the base of the shaft itself, which also housed elevators and stairs to bring passengers down to the eighty-sixth floor, where baggage and ticket areas would be located.
Another obstacle was the winds on top of the building were constantly shifting due to violent air currents.
Even if the dirigible were tethered to the mooring mast, the back of the ship would swivel around and around the mooring mast.

Dirigibles moored in open landing fields could be weighted down in the back with lead weights, but using these at the Empire State Building, where they would be dangling high above pedestrians on the street, was neither practical nor safe.
The other practical reason why dirigibles could not moor at the Empire State Building was an existing law against airships flying too low over urban areas.
This law would make it illegal for a ship to ever tie up to the building or even approach the area, although two dirigibles did attempt to reach the building before the entire idea was dropped.

The were many obstacle's the builder's of the Empire State Building had to face in attempt to allow the docking of dirigible's.
There was no way architects could drop a mooring mast on top of the building's smooth roof.
A thousand-foot dirigible moored at the top of the building, held by a single cable tether, would add stress to the building’s frame.
The stress of the dirigible’s load and the wind pressure would have to be transmitted all the way to the building’s foundation, which was nearly eleven hundred feet below.
The steel frame of the Empire State Building would have to be modified and strengthened to accommodate this new situation.
Over sixty thousand dollars’ worth of modifications had to be made to the building’s framework.
The greatest obstacle in launching this new design was nature.
Architects would needed to consider the constant shifting of winds due to violent air currents.
Even if the dirigible was tied to the mooring mast, the back of the ship would be unsturdy.
The fact that this design would be dangling above the pedestrians on the street, would worry the architects concern of the population.
Another problem was that most dirigibles from outside of the United States used hydrogen rather than helium, and hydrogen is highly flammable.
This would cause safety issues for the population below.
The other practical reason why dirigibles could not moor at the Empire State Building was an existing law against airships flying too low over urban areas.
This law would make it illegal for a ship to ever tie up to the building or even approach the area.
Even though two dirigibles attempted to reach the building, the idea of using the mooring mast was dropped.

In the end, the rooms in the Empire State Building that had been set aside for the ticketing and baggage of dirigible passengers were made over into the world’s highest soda fountain and tea garden for use by the sightseers who flocked to the observation decks.

The report alleges that police officers collaborated with a drug cartel in carrying out the abductions and killings, with some victims being burned alive.
The agency's investigation found that the police force failed to act to prevent the violence and even participated in the crimes.

KEY WEST, Fla. (AP) — Authorities say two men have been arrested in the 2010 theft of a museum's 17th-century gold bar, valued at $550,000.

A U.S. Department of Justice statement says 41-year-old Richard Steven Johnson, of Rio Linda, California, and 32-year-old Jarred Alexander Goldman, of Palm Beach Gardens, Florida, were arrested Monday and charged with conspiring to steal and stealing the gold bar from the Mel Fisher Maritime Heritage Museum in Key West.
It wasn't known if they have lawyers.
The 74.8-ounce (2.1-kilogram) bar was found in 1980 on a 1622 Spanish galleon wreck off the Florida Keys by the late shipwreck salvor Mel Fisher.
Authorities say it hasn't been recovered.
The theft of the gold bar in 2010 had puzzled investigators for years until recent developments led to the arrests of Johnson and Goldman.
The gold bar, which holds historical significance and substantial monetary value, has been a prized artifact at the Mel Fisher Maritime Heritage Museum.
The museum is known for its collection of treasures salvaged from shipwrecks in the area.
The community is eager for updates on the investigation and hopes for the safe return of the stolen gold bar.

I am not a patient person.

I get annoyed easily and I tend to lose my temper when things don't go my way.
There are a few girls in my team that completely kill my patience.
Am sure the other girls on my team feel the same way.
But there was this one time when I saw someone who was patient and it really impressed me.
She was always calm and composed, no matter what was happening around her.
One day, we were all hanging out at the mall and we decided to go to the ice cream shop.
There was a long line and we all started to get impatient.
But Lily just stood there quietly, waiting her turn.
When we finally got to the front of the line, they told us that they had run out of our favorite flavor.
I was so angry and disappointed, and I started to complain loudly.
But Lily just shrugged and said, "It's okay, we can try something new."
I was amazed at how she could be so patient and understanding.
Later that day, we went to the park to play some volleyball.
I was so annoyed with the girls who kept making mistakes and messing up our game.
But Lily just smiled and encouraged them, saying things like, "It's okay, we'll get it next time."
I realized then that being patient doesn't mean you don't get frustrated or annoyed.
It just means that you don't let those feelings control you.
From that day on, I tried to be more patient like Lily.
I still get annoyed sometimes, but I'm learning to take a deep breath and remind myself that things will work out in the end.
I'm also trying to be more understanding of other people's mistakes and shortcomings, instead of getting angry or upset.
In conclusion, patience is a virtue that not everyone possesses.
It's important to learn how to be patient in life, as it can help us deal with difficult situations and people.
And even if you're not a patient person by nature, you can always work on cultivating this trait and becoming a better, more understanding person.

In the story "Winter Hibiscus" by Minfong Ho, Saeng, a teenage girl, moves to the United States from Vietnam with her family.
After failing her driver's test, she sees a familiar plant, a hibiscus, and goes to a florist to see if she can purchase it.
The greenhouse reminds Saeng of her childhood in Vietnam, and she becomes overwhelmed with a wave of loss and weeps.
When she returns home, her mother is delighted with the plant, and they plant it together.
The story ends with Saeng vowing to retake her driver's test in the spring when the geese return and the hibiscus blooms.
Saeng's vow to retake her driver's test in the spring represents her determination to start anew and move forward in her new life in the United States.
She has been struggling with homesickness and the memories of her old life in Vietnam, but the hibiscus plant and her mother's encouragement have given her hope.
She realizes that she cannot change the past, but she can take control of her future and create new memories.
By vowing to retake the test in the spring, Saeng is showing that she is willing to keep trying and not give up.
In the paragraph at the very end of the story, Saeng is vowing that when nature and the world around her takes a fresh start, so will she in this new life.
She was saying that she will no longer be hung up on memories of the past but instead make new memories and be successful, thus having a new start.
The hibiscus plant represents this new beginning and hope for the future.
The plant is a "winter hibiscus," which means it can survive the cold winter months, just like Saeng can survive and thrive in her new home.
The geese returning in the spring also symbolize new beginnings and the cycle of life.
Saeng's vow to retake the test in the spring shows that she is ready to embrace this new chapter in her life and make the most of it.
Hey guys, have you ever experienced a moment where laughter was the only thing that could save the day?
I remember a time when I was in 7th grade, and my friends and I were working on a group project.
We were all so focused on getting our work done that we forgot to take a break and have some fun.
Suddenly, one of my friends let out a loud fart!
It was so unexpected that we all stopped what we were doing and looked at each other.
At first, we were all a little embarrassed, but then we started to laugh.
Before we knew it, we were all laughing so hard that our stomachs hurt.
After we finished laughing, we realized that we had been so stressed out about the project that we forgot to enjoy ourselves.
That moment of laughter brought us all closer together and gave us the energy we needed to finish our work.
Looking back on that moment, I realize how important it is to take a break and have a good laugh.
Laughter really is the best medicine!
It can bring people together and remind us of the simple joys in life.
I think that's why it's so important to keep laughter in our lives, even as we get older.
The simplicity of childhood is what makes it so precious.
Unfortunately as we all grown older, the future looms over our heads, casting a shadow over the things we cherish.
There is a predetermined way we are supposed to live our lives that for some reason, erases the plausibility of our true aspirations.
Laughter gives way to sighs and tears while dimples are forgotten and replaced with furrowed brows.
Everything in adulthood orbits around the office and is held to a nine to five obligation.
Businessmen walk past looking like identical mindless penguins.
Where did all the fun go?
But, we shouldn't let the stress of adulthood take away our laughter.
We should always find time to have a good laugh with our friends and family.
Laughter is what keeps us going and helps us forget about our problems, even if it's just for a moment.
When we laugh, we feel free and happy, and that's what life should be all about.
Instead we are confined to our felt paddock and swivel chair.
All the stress makes us forget to laugh, but we simply can't forget.
Laughter is the amnesia that makes the cubicle into a fort and the chair into a rocket ship that will take us from our fort to follow our dreams.
So when is the last time you got lost in laughter?
Take the pen and turn it into a quill.
Step out of your cubicle and find the world that you enjoy.
Laugh every day because life is too short to forget.

They needed to consult with experts and learn all they could about how dirigibles themselves worked.
It took engineers in New York and government workers all the way in Washington to piece together a plan on how to make it work.
Just adding the mast would never work.
Keeping it tethered by one cable would add a ton of stress to the framework, so all of the steel frame needed to be strengthened.

Dear Editor,  I believe that censorship in libraries is a bad idea.
I think that everyone should have the freedom to read whatever they want, regardless of whether or not someone else finds it offensive.
If we start censoring books, then where does it end?

This is a very important point.
If we start censoring books, then we will end up with nothing to read.

Many reasons kept dirigibles from docking on the top of the Empire State building.
Safety was a big issue that the builders had not considered.
The builders had not realized that the blimps use hydrogen.
Hydrogen is a gas that is highly flammable.
If a blimp caught fire it would be a catastrophe, especially in densely populated New York City.
Another obstacle was the changing winds on top of the building.
The winds were constantly shifting due to violent air currents.
Even if the dirigible were tethered to the mooring mast, the back of the ship would swivel around and around the mooring mast.

Dirigibles moored in open landing fields could be weighted down in the back with lead weights, but using these at the Empire State Building, where they would be dangling high above pedestrians on the street, was neither practical nor safe.
Lastly, an existing law against airships flying too low over urban areas would make it illegal for a ship to ever tie up to the building or even approach the area.
As a junior high school student, I strongly believe that censorship in libraries is not acceptable.
Everyone has the right to read whatever they want, and no one should be able to take that away from them.
If we start censoring books, where does it stop?
What's to say that the next book someone finds offensive won't be a book that I love?

Katherine Paterson, author of many beloved children's books, said it best when she stated, "All of us can think of a book that we hope none of our children or any other children have taken off the shelf.
But if I have the right to remove that book from the shelf -- that work I abhor -- then you also have exactly the same right and so does everyone else.
And then we have no books left on the shelf for any of us."
Censorship not only limits the availability of certain materials to the public, but it also limits creative freedom.

If the author of a book found out a local book store had removed the book they wrote, I think they would be pretty mad and they would possibly stop writing because they think people don't like what they write.
Censorship is not just a problem in books, but also in music, movies, and magazines.
Music is a way for people to express themselves, and if someone is offended by a particular song, they have the right to not listen to it.
However, they don't have the right to take that song off the airwaves.
Movies are a form of art, and if someone doesn't like a particular movie, they have the right to not watch it.
But they don't have the right to take that movie out of theaters.
Magazines are a source of information, and if someone finds a particular article offensive, they have the right to not read it.
But they don't have the right to take that magazine off the shelves.
The only way someone should be able to remove your work from being published or released is if the story talks about someone in particular in a bad way enough for the person to find it offensive.
One time I was at my local book store and a younger lady was looking down at a book that had a title that offended her.
She went and told the librarian and the next day the book had been removed from the library.
You shouldn't be able to do that.
If the lady found the book to be offensive she shouldn't have looked at it, she should have just ignored the book and kept on with what she was doing.
In my opinion, censorship is not acceptable.
People should be free to write what they want.
The author of the book shouldn't be blamed for writing offensive material, it should be the person finding it to be offensive that has the punishment.
If you don't like the book then don't read the book.

The builders of the Empire State Building faced several obstacles in attempting to allow dirigibles to dock there.
One of the greatest reasons was safety, as most dirigibles used hydrogen, which is highly flammable.
If the blimp was docked over a large city like New York City, it would be very dangerous if a blimp did catch on fire.
Another obstacle was that the docking system would not work as well as planned, nor would it be safe.
These airships are at the mercy of the winds and weather.
In normal cases of docking dirigibles on open landing fields, they are weighted down on the front and back.
However, using lead weights at the Empire State Building, where they would be dangling high above pedestrians on the street, was neither practical nor safe.
Additionally, the winds on top of the building were constantly shifting due to violent air currents.
Even if the dirigible were tethered to the mooring mast, the back of the ship would swivel around and around the mooring mast.
The other practical reason why dirigibles could not moor at the Empire State Building was an existing law against airships flying too low over urban areas.
This law would make it illegal for a ship to ever tie up to the building or even approach the area.

In the end, the idea of using the mooring mast was shelved, and the rooms in the Empire State Building that had been set aside for the ticketing and baggage of dirigible passengers were made over into the world’s highest soda fountain and tea garden for use by the sightseers who flocked to the observation decks.

Many people believe that laughter is a key part of any relationship.
There are many times when even the slightest laugh is needed to break the tension, or even just relieve some stress every once in a while.
It is often said that laughter is the best medicine, and also the cheapest.
Laughter is easily found and common to come by.
In my case, laughter comes naturally to my sister and I and for no particular reason at all; it not only saved, but it built our relationship to what it is today.
When we were younger, my older sister and I did not get along very well at all.
She would always tease me, then laugh about it; and I too would laugh at things that she did not find humorous in any way, shape, or form.
This constantly caused conflict and many arguments between the two of us; therefore we hated each other and, in a sense, wanted nothing to do with each other.
As my sister and I grew older and wiser, we started to become much more alike.
We still made fun of, teased, antagonized, and pulled childish pranks on each other; but instead of getting angry, we would just laugh about it instead.
As we continued to make each other laugh, we found ourselves getting along so much better.
One day, my sister and I decided to go to a water park together.
We were both excited to spend the day having fun and enjoying the sun.
However, things did not go as planned.
As soon as we got to the park, it started to rain.
Not just a little sprinkle, but a full-on downpour.
We were both soaked within minutes and were freezing cold.
We could have easily been angry and upset about the situation, but instead, we started to laugh.
We laughed at how ridiculous we looked, how we had traveled all this way just to get rained on, and how we were both shivering from the cold.
We decided to make the most of it and went on all the water rides.
The rain made it even more fun, and we were having a blast.
Before we knew it, my sister and I were best friends.
It is rare to hear about siblings being best friends.
I am lucky to be able to say that my older sister is my best friend.
Personally, I feel that laughter has played a huge roll in the relationship between my older sister and I.
Now we depend on each other because we both know that no matter what, we can always make one another laugh and virtually cheer each other up.
We hang out when we need to get away or when we have something that we need to get off our chests.
We know we have each other for that because we know we can always laugh about it in the end.

They couldn't way down the back using lead weights because it wasn't safe, so the builders needed to find an alternative.
Builders also faced the obstacle of the law.
It was against regulations to fly too low over urban areas.
This made it illegal for the blimp to approach the building, never mind docking at it.
For these practical reasons, dirigibles were never allowed to dock on the Empire State Building.
There were simply too many obstacles for the builders to overcome in order to make docking a success.

The Russian State Duma has put forward a controversial recommendation to classify journalists as 'foreign agents,' a move that has sparked concerns over press freedom in the country.

The proposal, made by the lower parliament's information committee, comes as an extension of a law enacted last year allowing Russia to label media organizations funded by foreign governments as foreign agents.
While this designation does not prohibit the outlets from operating, it does raise doubts about their impartiality and credibility.
The suggestion to require individual journalists to register as foreign agents has raised alarm bells among press freedom advocates, who fear it could have a chilling effect on independent reporting.
Critics argue that this move is part of a wider strategy by Russian authorities to restrict the free flow of information and undermine journalistic integrity.
Gulonoza Said of the Committee to Protect Journalists condemned the proposed law as a deliberate attempt to impede the work of journalists and stifle dissent.

The measure, which the lower parliament's information committee recommended on Tuesday, follows a law adopted last year under which Russia can designate media outlets receiving foreign government funding as foreign agents.
Naming an outlet as a foreign agent does not block its work but casts aspersions on its credibility.
Demanding that individual journalists register as agents could produce a chilling effect.

The proposed law "is the latest step in the Russian authorities' systematic policy towards obstructing the free flow of news," said Gulonoza Said of the Committee to Protect Journalists in a statement Tuesday.

LAKELAND, Fla. (AP) — A Florida man is suing his friend for misleading him about the value of his $1 million lottery ticket, and for pocketing the proceeds after helping him cash it in.
The Lakeland Ledger (http://bit.ly/2ssuIs8) reports 45-year-old John Rhoades asked his 28-year-old friend Tyler Scott for help after realizing the scratch-off ticket he bought in April was a winner.
Rhoades says he didn't know how much the ticket was worth or how to cash it in.
Rhoades claims that Scott told him the ticket was only worth $1,000 and offered to help him cash it in at a local convenience store.
Trusting his friend, Rhoades agreed, and Scott indeed cashed in the ticket on his behalf.
However, Rhoades later discovered that the ticket was actually worth $1 million.
Feeling betrayed and taken advantage of, Rhoades has filed a lawsuit against Scott, alleging fraud and seeking the rightful amount of the winnings.
Scott, on the other hand, denies any wrongdoing and insists that he was simply helping out a friend in need.
As the legal battle unfolds, the true nature of their friendship and the outcome of the case remain uncertain.

The builders of the Empire State Building faced many obstacles in attempting to allow dirigibles to dock there.
One of the reasons was safety.
Most dirigibles from outside of the United States used hydrogen rather than helium, and hydrogen is highly flammable.
This presented a risk of fire above a densely populated area such as downtown New York.

Even if the dirigible were tethered to the mooring mast, the back of the ship would swivel around and around the mooring mast.

Dirigibles moored in open landing fields could be weighted down in the back with lead weights, but using these at the Empire State Building, where they would be dangling high above pedestrians on the street, was neither practical nor safe.
The existing law against airships flying too low over urban areas was also an obstacle.
This law would make it illegal for a ship to ever tie up to the building or even approach the area.

Censorship in libraries is not a good idea.
Some people think that books, music, movies, magazines, and other materials should be removed from the shelves if they are found offensive.
But I believe that this is not a good thing to do.
First of all, everyone has different opinions and beliefs.
Some people might find a book offensive, but others might not.
If we start to remove books just because some people find them offensive, then we are limiting our own freedom to read and learn.
We should be able to read books that challenge us and make us think, even if they make us uncomfortable.
Secondly, censorship can lead to a slippery slope.
If we start to remove books, then where do we draw the line?
Who gets to decide what is offensive and what is not?
If we give one person or group the power to censor, then others will want the same power.
This can lead to a situation where there are no books left on the shelves at all.
Lastly, if something is just stating facts, it should be left alone.
If it is just stating facts it should be left alone, but if it is considered to be just a false report it should be removed.

And then we have no books left on the shelf for any of us."
I think this is true because if we start to take books off the shelves because we don't like them, then other people will start doing the same thing.
Soon, there will be no books left in the library.
This is not a good thing because books help us learn about the world and ourselves.
We need to be able to read books that challenge us and make us think.
In the story "Winter Hibiscus" by Minfong Ho, Saeng moves to the United States from Vietnam with her family.
She feels homesick and struggles to adjust to her new life.
However, when she sees a hibiscus plant, she is reminded of her childhood in Vietnam and feels a sense of familiarity.
Later, Saeng buys the plant and plants it in her garden.
At the end of the story, Saeng vows to retake her driver's test in the spring when the snow melts and the geese return.
This shows that she is starting to accept her new life and is willing to move forward.
The hibiscus plant represents a connection to Saeng's past and helps her realize that there are similarities between her old country and her new one.
Up until this point Saeng had been lamenting her old country, and not adjusting well to her new one.
The Hibiscus inspires her, and lets her know that the new country has many of the same things as her old country.
In this last line, she comes to terms with her present situation.
"When the snows melts and the geese return and this hibiscus is budding," is a way of saying shes going to let a little time pass, and by taking her driver’s test again, she will begin her new life.

Many forms of literature is found to be offensive, especially adults' sections that are provided only for their entertainment.
But sometimes children sway from their shelves, that are censored for their well-being, and to an inappropriate section.
I believe that these certain books should not be provided in a public library where children go with their parents.
I know how curious children are, especially at my sister's age.
She is only nine-years-old, but she is slowly making her way to being a young adolecent and has strayed into adult territory in the library many times.
Most of these books have inappropriate language, scenes of 'love-making', and violence.

Of course people say that children at her age are supposed to learn these aspects of life on their own, but why should she accidentally read a book that has these certain aspects and then consider it okay?
If an adult wants a certain book like that then they should buy it for themselves and hide it away from pure minds.

However, if an individual cannot afford to buy their books for themselves then either a library for adults should be made, or special sections in libraries could be fenced off that only adults can enter.
Even magazines, I think, should be censored.
Most magazines are not based on a child's mind.
They are made for gossip and are more suitable for an adult's mind-set.
Especially the ones about celebrity relationships, drama, drugs, and alcohol.
We should be trying to teach our children not subject them to ideas of corruption that society thrusts upon them.
Society can be cruel to whoever is thrown out into it.
That is why we prepare our children: to be ready to go out on their own.
However, from these books they learn too early.
I remember when I was younger, I stumbled across a book that had a scene of love-making.
At the moment, I had no clue what was happening.
But later on, when I grew up and read the book again, I realized what had happened.
I wish I never read that book when I was younger.
In conclusion, censorship in libraries is important for children's well-being.
Children are curious and do not understand the consequences of reading books with inappropriate content.
Therefore, books that contain inappropriate language, scenes of 'love-making', and violence should not be provided in public libraries.
Instead, there should be a separate section for adults or libraries for adults should be made.

Censorship in libraries is something that should be taken rather seriously.
I beleive that children should have the freedom to read whatever book they pick off of the shelf.
We should not put limits on our children's books that they are allowed to read.
Growing up as a child, there was no one to tell me what books I could and could not read.
Children are not oblivious to the world, and sooner or later they are going to figure stuff out.
I think that maybe we could put a censorship on movies and magazines that you can get, but not books.
When I was little, one of the ways I learned what I know now was from reading.
Books have always been a gateway for children to explore different worlds and ideas.
I remember when I was younger; I would read books about different cultures and countries, and it would open my eyes to the world outside my own.
If we start censoring books, then we are limiting a child's ability to learn and explore different topics.
We should not put a limit on what children can read because that is not fair to them.
They should be able to read whatever interests them and learn from it.
Censorship in libraries can also lead to a slippery slope.
If we start censoring books, then what is stopping us from censoring other forms of media?
We can't just pick and choose what we want children to see and read.
It's not fair to them, and it's not fair to the creators of the content.
Everyone should have the right to express themselves through their work, and it's up to the individual to decide whether or not they want to engage with it.
Katherine Paterson, the author of many popular children's books, once said, "All of us can think of a book that we hope none of our children or any other children have taken off the shelf.
But if I have the right to remove that book from the shelf -- that work I abhor -- then you also have exactly the same right, and so does everyone else.
And then we have no books left on the shelf for any of us."
This quote perfectly sums up why censorship in libraries is not the answer.
If we start removing books that we find offensive, then eventually, there will be no books left on the shelves for anyone to read.
In conclusion, censorship in libraries is not the answer.
Children should have the freedom to read whatever book they want, and we should not put limits on what they can and cannot read.
Books are a gateway for children to explore different worlds and ideas, and we should not limit their ability to learn and grow.
Censorship can lead to a slippery slope, and we should not start picking and choosing what content we want children to see and read.
We should trust our children to make their own decisions and learn from their experiences.

The next phase of Longbridge's ongoing regeneration project has been unveiled, marking another significant step in the rejuvenation of the area.
The new development plans promise to bring further growth and opportunity to this historic town.
Regeneration specialist St Modwen has revealed their vision for a new two-storey office building, named 3 Devon Way, situated off Longbridge Lane.
This modern complex is set to cover an impressive 26,260 sq ft and will include an additional 80 parking spaces on top of the existing car park facilities.
The construction of 3 Devon Way is expected to generate around 165 new job opportunities within the town, providing a welcome boost to the local economy.

Strategically located next to 2 Devon Way and the Innovation Centre, the new office building will form an integral part of the Longbridge Technology Park, contributing to the overall £1 billion town centre regeneration initiative that was initiated following the closure of MG Rover in 2005.
In a recent development, St Modwen has shifted its focus from the previously planned cinema project in Longbridge to explore new opportunities.
The decision to abandon the cinema plans was attributed to prevailing market conditions that hindered the feasibility of the project.
As a result, the developer is now seeking approval to construct a discount supermarket on a vacant plot opposite Sainsbury's and Marks & Spencer stores.

It is expected the new complex will create 165 jobs in the town.

But it has emerged the plans were dropped by St Modwen as the company said market conditions meant it had not been possible to carry out this project.

No, a better piece of advice for the solo cyclist would be, “Never accept travel advice from a collection of old-timers who haven’t left the confines of their porches since Carter was in office.” It’s not that a group of old guys doesn’t know the terrain.
With age comes wisdom and all that, but the world is a fluid place.
Had he been driving through, say, a forest or perhaps rolling grasslands, he might not have been in such danger, and could have merely looked for a river or dreck for water if he was desperate.
Another thing that might have affected the cyclist would have been the affect of the desert on his mind.
When people think of deserts they often think of dry, barren wastelands, complete with buzzards and maybe a dead cowskull, as in movies.

Deserts are in intimidiating, they have a bad reputation and so, as he was riding through and was low on water thought of death how he was, "going to die and the birds would pick (him) clean" running through his now-teriffied head.
Had he been in a city or in rolling farmland he might not have been as terrified.
At a reservoir campground outside of Lodi, California, the cyclist enjoyed the serenity of an early-summer evening and some lively conversation with a group of old codgers.
What he shouldn’t have done was let them have a peek at his map.
Like a foolish youth, the next morning he followed their advice and launched out at first light along a “shortcut” that was to slice away hours from his ride to Yosemite National Park.
The cyclist rode into the morning with strong legs and a smile on his face.
However, things began to change soon.
After forty miles into the pedal, he arrived at the first “town” which was a ghost town.
The sun was beginning to beat down, but he barely noticed it.
The cool pines and rushing rivers of Yosemite had his name written all over them.
Twenty miles up the road, he came to a fork of sorts.
One ramshackle shed, several rusty pumps, and a corral that couldn’t hold in the lamest mule greeted him.
He had been hitting his water bottles pretty regularly, and he was traveling through the high deserts of California in June.

The cyclist tried to pump the handle of the rusted water pump with all his strength but a tarlike substance oozed out, followed by brackish water feeling somewhere in the neighborhood of two hundred degrees.
The old guys had sworn the next town was only eighteen miles down the road.
He would conserve his water and go inward for an hour or so—a test of his inner spirit.
Not two miles into this next section of the ride, he noticed the terrain changing.
Flat road was replaced by short, rolling hills.
After he had crested the first few of these, a large highway sign jumped out at him.
It read: ROUGH ROAD AHEAD: DO NOT EXCEED POSTED SPEED LIMIT.
The cyclist was doing a water-depleting 12 mph.
Sometimes life can feel so cruel.
At some point, tumbleweeds crossed his path and a ridiculously large snake blocked the majority of the pavement in front of him.
The water bottles contained only a few tantalizing sips.

Wide rings of dried sweat circled his shirt, and the growing realization that he could drop from heatstroke on a gorgeous day in June simply because he listened to some gentlemen who hadn’t been off their porch in decades, caused him to laugh.
It was a sad, hopeless laugh, mind you, but at least he still had the energy to feel sorry for himself.
There was no one in sight, not a building, car, or structure of any kind.
He began breaking the ride down into distances he could see on the horizon, telling himself that if he could make it that far, he’d be fine.
Over one long, crippling hill, a building came into view.
The cyclist wiped the sweat from his eyes to make sure it wasn’t a mirage, and tried not to get too excited.
With what he believed was his last burst of energy, he maneuvered down the hill.
In an ironic twist that should please all sadists reading this, the building—abandoned years earlier, by the looks of it—had been a Welch’s Grape Juice factory and bottling plant.
A sandblasted picture of a young boy pouring a refreshing glass of juice into his mouth could still be seen.

As the cyclist stumbled into a rather modern bathroom and drank deeply from the sink, he had an overwhelming urge to seek out Gary and Wilber, kiss them, and buy some bait—any bait, even though he didn’t own a rod or reel.
An old guy sitting in a chair under some shade nodded in his direction.
Cool water dripped from his head as he slumped against the wall beside him.
“Where you headed in such a hurry?” “Yosemite,” he whispered.
“Know the best way to get there?” The cyclist watched him from the corner of his eye for a long moment.
He was even older than the group he’d listened to in Lodi.
I own a very good map.” And he promised himself right then that he’d always stick to it in the future.

Censorship is a topic that has been debated for years.
Should certain materials, such as books, music, movies, magazines, etc., be removed from the shelves if they are found offensive?
In my opinion, I believe that censorship in libraries is not the answer.
As Katherine Paterson, author of Bridge to Terabithia, stated, "All of us can think of a book that we hope none of our children or any other children have taken off the shelf.
But if I have the right to remove that book from the shelf -- that work I abhor -- then you also have exactly the same right and so does everyone else.
And then we have no books left on the shelf for any of us."
This quote perfectly sums up my thoughts on censorship.
If we begin to remove books that we find offensive, soon there will be nothing left on the shelves for anyone to read.
However, there is a definite line that reaches over to offensiveness that can easily be crossed by authors across the globe.
In my experience, I have seen people who are easily offended by certain materials.
They believe that these materials promote negative stereotypes and can be damaging to certain groups of people.
However, I have also seen people who believe that censorship is a violation of their rights.
They feel that they have the right to read and express their opinions freely, without fear of censorship.
I believe that both sides have valid points, but we must find a balance between the two.
If a person is offended by something someone wrote, they should just avoid reading it.
However, this does not give authors the power to target a group in their writing and offend them specifically.
This is a very two-sided subject.
It can not strictly be controlled by censoring libraries; it is also in the hands of authors and readers everywhere.
Authors and media producers should take other people into consideration and put their efforts into raising awareness instead of offending.
In regards to this, readers across the globe should keep in mind why the author might target them, and avoid conflict by avoiding the material.

All the new technology has hurt them and its not likely that they will ever become more prominent than other reasources, like the internet, again.With this in mind, how much would censoring libraries really help those offended groups in the world?
Most likely, they would not even notice a change.
Everyone has the right to have an opinon and share it, but it is important to keep the feelings of others in mind as well.

Do you bleieve that certain materials, such as books, music, movies, magazines, etc., should be removed from the shelves if they are found offensive?'
In my opinion, censorship is a tricky subject.
While it may seem like a good idea to remove offensive materials from shelves, it can lead to a dangerous path of limiting people's access to information and ideas.
We need variety of all books, music, movies, magazines, etc.. Censorship is understandable, in some ways.
For example, if a book or movie is promoting illegal activities or causing harm, it should not be allowed.
However, if someone does not like a book or movie, they have the right to not read or watch it.
Katherine Paterson, author of Bridge to Terabithia, said, "All of us can think of a book that we hope none of our children or any other children have taken off the shelf.
But if I have the right to remove that book from the shelf -- that work I abhor -- then you also have exactly the same right and so does everyone else.
And then we have no books left on the shelf for any of us".
This means that if we start removing books that some people find offensive, eventually there will be no books left for anyone.
In addition, reading books that may be considered offensive can help people understand different perspectives and cultures.
For example, To Kill a Mockingbird by Harper Lee is a classic book that has been banned in some schools because of its use of racial slurs.
However, this book helps people understand the struggles of African Americans during the Jim Crow era.
Music and movies are also forms of art that should not be censored.
Just because someone finds a song or movie offensive does not mean it should be removed.
People have different tastes and opinions.
If someone does not like a certain song or movie, they have the choice to not listen or watch it.
In conclusion, censorship should only be used in extreme cases where the material is promoting illegal activities or causing harm.
Everyone has the right to their own opinion and should not force their beliefs on others.
We need a variety of books, music, movies, magazines, etc.
to help us understand different perspectives and cultures.

From that day on, I started to appreciate patience more.
I realized that being patient doesn't just mean waiting for things.
It means enjoying the journey, even if it takes a long time.
It means being understanding and tolerant of others, even when they make mistakes.
It means experiencing difficulties without complaining and finding joy in the little things.

As a student, I strongly believe that censorship in libraries is not the solution to the problem of offensive materials.
While it is understandable that some people may find certain materials, such as books, music, movies, magazines, etc., offensive, it is not fair to remove them from the shelves for everyone else.

As Katherine Paterson, author of many famous children's books, says, "if I have the right to remove that book from the shelf - that work I abhor - then you also have exactly the same right and so does everyone else.
And then we have no books left on the shelf for any of us."
One of the main reasons why censorship is not the answer is because it limits our freedom of expression.
Everyone has the right to express their opinions and ideas, and this includes artists and authors.
By censoring their work, we are essentially silencing their voices and preventing them from sharing their perspectives with the world.
Furthermore, censorship can also lead to a lack of diversity in our libraries.
If certain materials are removed, then we are only left with a narrow range of perspectives and ideas.
This can be detrimental to our education and personal growth.
Moreover, censorship can also have a negative impact on our critical thinking skills.
When we are exposed to controversial materials, we are forced to think critically about the issues at hand.
We are encouraged to form our own opinions and to question the status quo.
By censoring these materials, we are preventing ourselves from engaging in these important conversations and debates.
Of course, there are some materials that should be protected from children.
However, this should not be a blanket rule for all offensive materials.
Parents and guardians should take responsibility for monitoring what their children are exposed to and guiding them through difficult topics.
It is not the responsibility of libraries to act as censors for every family.
In conclusion, censorship in libraries is not the answer to the problem of offensive materials.
It limits our freedom of expression, reduces diversity, and hinders our critical thinking skills.
While some materials may need to be protected from children, this should not be a blanket rule for all offensive materials.
As a society, we should encourage open and honest conversations about difficult topics, rather than trying to hide them away.
War should definitely be one of those subjects people be exposed to.
People are dieing for us everyday, so we should know more about it.
By censoring materials related to war, we are essentially ignoring the sacrifices of our brave soldiers and the impact of war on our society.
It is important for us to understand the complexities of war and to have open and honest conversations about the subject.

He represented John L. Brady in the landmark case that established the "Brady rule," requiring prosecutors to disclose exculpatory evidence to the defense.
This ruling has had a significant impact on the criminal justice system, ensuring that defendants receive a fair trial.

His legacy will continue to inspire future generations of legal professionals to strive for justice and equality in the legal system.

Today, I want to talk about censorship in libraries.
As Katherine Paterson, author of Bridge to Terabithia, said, "All of us can think of a book that we hope none of our children or any other children have taken off the shelf.
But if I have the right to remove that book from the shelf -- that work I abhor -- then you also have exactly the same right and so does everyone else.
And then we have no books left on the shelf for any of us."
I believe that censorship in libraries is wrong.
It is not fair to remove books, music, movies, or magazines just because some people find them offensive.
Everyone has different opinions and beliefs, and it is important to respect them.
When we censor materials, we are limiting people's access to information and ideas.
We are preventing them from learning about different cultures, perspectives, and experiences.
We are also taking away their freedom of choice.
In my own experience, I have read books that some people might find offensive.
For example, I read The Catcher in the Rye by J.D.
Some parents and teachers wanted to ban the book because of its language and themes.
However, I think it was an important book for me to read because it helped me understand teenage angst and rebellion.
I also believe that parents should be responsible for what their children read, watch, or listen to.
They should talk to their children about their values and beliefs and help them make informed decisions.
In conclusion, censorship in libraries is not the answer.
We should allow people to read, watch, or listen to whatever they choose.
We should respect their opinions and beliefs, even if we do not agree with them.

From the idea of building the Empire State Building to attempting to allow dirigibles to dock there, the builders faced different obstacles while attempting to allow dirigibles to dock there.
Al Smith thought it was a good idea to add a mooring mast so dirigibles could dock there for several hours.
However, there were some obstacles that the builders faced while attempting to allow dirigibles to dock there.
One of the main obstacles was safety.
Most dirigibles from outside of the United States used hydrogen rather than helium, and hydrogen is highly flammable.
This made it dangerous to allow dirigibles to dock at the Empire State Building, especially since it was located in a densely populated area.
The other obstacle was the wind.
The strength of the wind were constantly shifting due to violent air currents.
Even if the dirigible was tethered to the mooring mast, the back of the ship would swivel around the mast.
Dirigibles moored in open landing fields could be weighted down in the back with lead weights, but using these at the Empire State Building was neither practical nor safe.
The other practical reason why dirigibles could not moor at the Empire State Building was an existing law against airships flying too low over urban areas.
This law would make it illegal for a ship to ever tie up to the building or even approach the area, although two dirigibles did attempt to reach the building before the entire idea was dropped.

In February 1931, Irving Clavan of the building’s architectural office said, “The as yet unsolved problems of mooring air ships to a fixed mast at such a height made it desirable to postpone to a later date the final installation of the landing gear.” By the late 1930s, the idea of using the mooring mast for dirigibles and their passengers had quietly disappeared.
