The builders of the Empire State Building faced several obstacles in attempting to allow dirigibles to dock there.
First, the stress of a dirigible's load and wind pressure would have to be transmitted all the way to the building’s foundation, which was nearly eleven hundred feet below.
This meant that the steel frame of the building would have to be modified and strengthened to accommodate this new situation.
Over sixty thousand dollars’ worth of modifications had to be made to the building’s framework.
Furthermore, the winds on top of the building were constantly shifting due to violent air currents.
Even if the dirigible were tethered to the mooring mast, the back of the ship would swivel around and around the mooring mast.
This made it difficult for dirigibles to dock and for passengers to safely get on and off the dirigible by walking down a gangplank to an open observation platform.
Another obstacle was an existing law against airships flying too low over urban areas.
This law would make it illegal for a ship to ever tie up to the building or even approach the area.
Because of the location, the winds were so strong and the wind shifted constantly.

Despite the challenges, the architects of the Empire State Building designed a shiny glass and chrome-nickel stainless steel tower that would be illuminated from inside, with a stepped-back design that imitated the overall shape of the building itself.
The rocket-shaped mast would have four wings at its corners, of shiny aluminum, and would rise to a conical roof that would house the mooring arm.

The winches and control machinery for the dirigible mooring would be housed in the base of the shaft itself, which also housed elevators and stairs to bring passengers down to the eighty-sixth floor, where baggage and ticket areas would be located.
However, by the late 1930s, the idea of using the mooring mast for dirigibles and their passengers had quietly disappeared.
Dirigibles, instead of becoming the transportation of the future, had given way to airplanes.

The rooms in the Empire State Building that had been set aside for the ticketing and baggage of dirigible passengers were made over into the world’s highest soda fountain and tea garden for use by the sightseers who flocked to the observation decks.
The highest open observation deck, intended for disembarking passengers, has never been open to the public.
By the late nineteen thirtie's, the idea landing dirigibles on the Empire State Building disappeared.
Instead, the idea of air transportation was given to airplanes.

As a student, I believe that censorship in libraries is a complicated issue.
On the one hand, I understand why some people might want certain materials removed from the shelves.
After all, there are books, music, movies, and magazines out there that contain content that is offensive or inappropriate for certain audiences.
However, I also believe that censorship can be a slippery slope.
If we start removing materials simply because they offend someone, where do we draw the line?
Will anything that someone finds offensive be fair game for censorship?
Katherine Paterson, the author of many books for young readers, once said, "All of us can think of a book that we hope none of our children or any other children have taken off the shelf.
But if I have the right to remove that book from the shelf -- that work I abhor -- then you also have exactly the same right and so does everyone else.
And then we have no books left on the shelf for any of us."
I think this statement is very powerful because it highlights the dangers of censorship.
If we start removing materials simply because they offend us, we risk losing access to a wide range of perspectives and ideas.
Of course, that's not to say that we should never remove anything from library shelves.
If something is truly harmful or dangerous, then it may be necessary to take action.
But I think it's important to approach this issue with caution and to consider the potential consequences of censorship.
There are two main arguments that I've heard in favor of censorship.
The first is that certain materials are simply too offensive or inappropriate for certain audiences, especially children.
While I understand this argument, I think it's important to remember that everyone has different ideas about what is offensive or inappropriate.
What one person finds offensive, another might not.
And who gets to decide what is and isn't appropriate for certain audiences?
I think it's dangerous to give any one group too much power over what we can and cannot access.
The second argument I've heard in favor of censorship is that people who are offended by certain materials should simply avoid them.
While this might seem like a reasonable solution, I think it's important to remember that offensive or inappropriate materials are all around us.
If we start removing everything that offends someone, we'll be left with very little.
And again, who gets to decide what is and isn't offensive?
In conclusion, I believe that censorship in libraries is a complicated issue.

The builders of the Empire State Building faced several obstacles in attempting to allow dirigibles to dock there.
One of the biggest problems was safety.
Most dirigibles from outside the United States used hydrogen, which is highly flammable.

When the German dirigible Hindenburg was destroyed by fire in New Jersey in 1937, the owners of the Empire State Building realized how much worse that accident could have been if it had taken place above a densely populated area such as downtown New York.
Another issue was the constantly shifting winds on top of the building due to violent air currents.
Even if the dirigible were tethered to the mooring mast, the back of the ship would swivel around and around the mast.

Dirigibles moored in open landing fields could be weighted down in the back with lead weights, but using these at the Empire State Building, where they would be dangling high above pedestrians on the street, was neither practical nor safe.
Additionally, there was an existing law against airships flying too low over urban areas, which would make it illegal for a ship to ever tie up to the building or even approach the area.
Also, the architects had to plan out how they would attach a winch and other things to get the dirigible to stay on the mast.
The builders had to build four wings at the corners of the mast, that would rise to a conical roof to house the mooring arm.
Lastly, the architects had to figure out the winches and control machinery for the dirigibles and where they would be housed to accommodate it.
These are a few obstacles the builders had to face in attempting to allow dirigibles to dock at the Empire State Building.

Censorship in libraries is a hotly debated topic.
Some argue that certain materials, such as books, music, movies, and magazines, should be removed from the shelves if they are found offensive.
Others believe that censorship is a violation of our freedom of speech and expression.
In my opinion, censorship is not the answer to the problem.
As Katherine Paterson, the author of Bridge to Terabithia, once said, "All of us can think of a book that we hope none of our children or any other children have taken off the shelf.
But if I have the right to remove that book from the shelf -- that work I abhor -- then you also have exactly the same right and so does everyone else.
And then we have no books left on the shelf for any of us."
If we start removing books or any other materials from libraries based on our personal opinions, where do we draw the line?
Who decides what is offensive or inappropriate?
What if one person's idea of offensive material differs from someone else's?
Furthermore, censorship often leads to a lack of diversity in our reading materials.
It is important to have access to a wide range of perspectives and ideas, even if we don't always agree with them.
Reading controversial books and other materials can help us understand different viewpoints and learn more about the world around us.

STOP-DWI Coordinator Chris Marion confirmed the Chris Thater Memorial Race will not take place this August.

The races for amateur and professional cyclists were created in honor of Chris Thater, a 23-year-old cycling enthusiast and Binghamton University graduate who was killed by a drunk driver near Harpursville in 1983.
The decision to cancel the event was made due to ongoing concerns and uncertainties surrounding the COVID-19 pandemic.
Organizers expressed their disappointment in having to call off the race, recognizing the significance of the event not only in the local community but also in the broader cycling world.
The Chris Thater Memorial Race has been a staple in the Binghamton area, drawing cyclists and spectators from near and far to celebrate the sport and honor Chris Thater's memory.

Despite the cancellation, organizers are optimistic about the event returning in the future and are exploring alternative ways to engage with the community and support cycling enthusiasts during these challenging times.

The race's impact on promoting cycling safety and awareness of the dangers of drunk driving remains a crucial aspect of its legacy, and efforts will continue to uphold these important messages even in the absence of this year's physical event.

Today, I want to talk about censorship in libraries.
I believe that certain materials, such as books, music, movies, magazines, etc., should not be removed from the shelves just because some people find them offensive.
As Katherine Paterson, author of Bridge to Terabithia, said: "All of us can think of a book that we hope none of our children or any other children have taken off the shelf.
But if I have the right to remove that book from the shelf -- that work I abhor -- then you also have exactly the same right and so does everyone else.
And then we have no books left on the shelf for any of us."

This means that if we allow some people to censor materials they find offensive, then everyone else will also have the same right, and eventually, there will be no materials left for anyone to read or view.
That's why we are allowed to take off a book from the shelf.
Most important reason is that the people are want to know many knowledges.
Censorship limits our access to knowledge and different perspectives.
We cannot grow as individuals and as a society if we only read or view materials that align with our own beliefs and values.
By exposing ourselves to diverse ideas and opinions, we can broaden our understanding of the world and become more empathetic towards others.
Furthermore, censorship can be a slippery slope.
Once we start censoring one type of material, it can lead to the censorship of other materials that may not necessarily be offensive but may challenge the status quo.
This can stifle creativity and innovation, and also limit our ability to have important conversations about social issues.
In conclusion, I believe that censorship in libraries should be avoided.
It is important to have access to diverse materials that may challenge our beliefs and values, as this is essential for personal and societal growth.
Thank you for reading my essay.
I hope you can understand my perspective on censorship in libraries.

The builders of the Empire State Building faced several obstacles in attempting to allow dirigibles to dock there.
First they had to make sure the dirigible wouldn't tear down the framework of the building.
Because the dirigible was so large and heavy the dirigible added with the wind would "be transmitted all the way to the building's foundation" which was at the bottom.
This had to be addressed, or the building would have been destroyed.

The architects designed a shiny glass and chrome-nickel stainless steel tower that would be illuminated from inside, with a stepped-back design that imitated the overall shape of the building itself.
However, the greatest obstacle to the successful use of the mooring mast was nature itself.
The winds on top of the building were constantly shifting due to violent air currents.
Even if the dirigible were tethered to the mooring mast, the back of the ship would swivel around and around the mooring mast.

Dirigibles moored in open landing fields could be weighted down in the back with lead weights, but using these at the Empire State Building, where they would be dangling high above pedestrians on the street, was neither practical nor safe.

The builders of the Empire State Building faced many obstacles in attempting to allow dirigibles to dock there.
Most dirigibles used hydrogen, which is highly flammable.
If an accident happened while a dirigible was docked at the top of the building, it could have catastrophic consequences in the densely populated area of downtown New York.
Another challenge was the constant shifting winds on top of the building due to violent air currents.
Even if a dirigible was tethered to the mooring mast, the back of the ship would swivel around and around the mast.

Dirigibles moored in open landing fields could be weighted down in the back with lead weights, but using these at the Empire State Building, where they would be dangling high above pedestrians on the street, was neither practical nor safe.
Finally, there was an existing law against airships flying too low over urban areas, which would make it illegal for a ship to ever tie up to the building or even approach the area.
Despite these challenges, the architects of the Empire State Building designed a shiny glass and chrome-nickel stainless steel tower that would be illuminated from inside.
The rocket-shaped mast would have four wings at its corners, of shiny aluminum, and would rise to a conical roof that would house the mooring arm.

The winches and control machinery for the dirigible mooring would be housed in the base of the shaft itself, which also housed elevators and stairs to bring passengers down to the eighty-sixth floor, where baggage and ticket areas would be located.
However, the mooring mast of the Empire State Building was destined to never fulfill its purpose.
Most dirigibles from outside of the United States used hydrogen rather than helium, and hydrogen is highly flammable.
The winds on top of the building were constantly shifting due to violent air currents, making it impossible for a dirigible to safely dock there.
Additionally, there was an existing law against airships flying too low over urban areas, which would make it illegal for a ship to ever tie up to the building or even approach the area.

The author's decision to follow the advice of a group of old men who hadn't left their porches for decades leads him to a rough road ahead.
The setting of the high deserts of California adds a sense of urgency to his trip when he starts to run low on water.
The author's struggle to find clean water and the fear of heatstroke demonstrate how the setting affects the cyclist.
He writes that the water pump produced brackish water, which was like battery acid.
The lack of water made it difficult for him to continue his journey.
In addition, the rolling hills in the terrain made it even harder for him to progress.
The author's experience shows that the setting of a journey can make or break the trip.
In conclusion, the setting of the story presents the main points of conflict to the author and thus was essential to the essay.

I remember a time when I was patient.
It was when I went to the doctor's office for a check-up.
I was feeling nervous because I didn't like getting shots.
When I got to the office, the nurse took my temperature and weight, and then the doctor came in.
He asked me some questions and then said that he needed to give me a shot.
I started to get scared and wanted to leave, but my mom told me to be brave and that it would be over quickly.
The doctor left the room to get the shot, but he was taking a long time.
I was being patient because the doctor was looking for a needle to stick in my arm.
He told me to wait a second, but I wasn’t waiting a second I was waiting for hours.
My mom couldn’t wait any longer she was about to take me home.
I told her to be patient and it would fill like time is going faster .She said, she is going to try, but if it didn’t work were leaving.
She waited patiently and next thing you know the doctor came back in the room and said thanks for being patient.
I was so happy that the doctor gave me a sucker.
My mom was happy too that we didn't have to come back for another appointment.
She told me that I was very brave and patient.
I was proud of myself because I didn't cry or complain even though I was scared.
Being patient is important because it helps us to get through difficult situations without getting upset.
Sometimes things take longer than we want them to, but if we are patient, we can get through them without feeling frustrated.
It's like waiting for a cake to bake in the oven.
You can't rush it because it won't turn out right.
You have to be patient and wait for it to be done.
I learned that being patient can be hard sometimes, but it's worth it in the end.
It can help us to get what we want and avoid unnecessary stress.
I hope that I can be patient in the future, just like I was at the doctor's office.

When constructing the mooring mast, the builders of the Empire State Building faced many obstacles in attempting to allow dirigibles to dock there.
One of the biggest challenges was the fact that the building was not originally designed to accommodate a mooring mast, so modifications had to be made to strengthen the steel frame of the building.

Additionally, the designers had to ensure that the mast was not just functional but also aesthetically pleasing, so they created a shiny glass and chrome-nickel stainless steel tower that imitated the overall shape of the building itself.
However, the biggest obstacles to the successful use of the mooring mast were safety concerns and the unpredictable winds at the top of the building.

Most dirigibles used hydrogen, which is highly flammable, and the owners of the Empire State Building realized how dangerous it would be to have a dirigible accident above a densely populated area such as downtown New York.
Furthermore, the winds on top of the building were constantly shifting due to violent air currents, making it difficult for dirigibles to safely dock at the mast.
The back of the ship would swivel around and around the mooring mast, and the use of lead weights to counterbalance the ship was not practical or safe.
Lastly, there ""was an existing law against airships flying too low over urban areas"" which prevented any dirigible to tie up to the building.
""The mooring mast of the Empire State Building was destined to never fulfill its purpose,"" for these obstacles were too great to surpass.

The stress that the dirigible's load and the wind pressure would have to be transmitted all the way to the building's foundation, which was nearly eleven hundred feet below.
To accommodate this new situation, the steel frame of the Empire State Building would have to be modified and strengthened, which cost over sixty thousand dollars.
Another obstacle was the constantly shifting winds on top of the building due to violent air currents.
Even if the dirigible were tethered to the mooring mast, the back of the ship would swivel around and around the mooring mast.
Additionally, existing laws against airships flying too low over urban areas would make it illegal for a ship to ever tie up to the building or even approach the area.

In our world today, there is a way to find anything that you could ever want under one roof.
Libraries are a great example of this.
They have books, movies, music, magazines, and even internet access.
However, there are some people who believe that certain materials should be removed from the shelves if they are found offensive.
Yes, the libraries do have blocks on the internet for websites that are very outragously offensive, but people have learned how to get around the blocks.
Libraries are set up to where all the kids materials is in one location, all the teenage stuff is in another spot, and all the adult materials are in another room.
Censorship is a controversial issue that has been debated for many years.
Some people believe that certain materials, such as books, music, movies, and magazines, should be removed from the shelves if they are found offensive.
However, I believe that censorship is wrong and that we should not remove materials from libraries just because some people find them offensive.
Firstly, censorship violates our freedom of speech and expression.
The First Amendment of the United States Constitution guarantees us the right to freedom of speech and expression.
This means that we have the right to express our opinions, ideas, and beliefs without fear of censorship or retaliation.
By removing materials from libraries, we are limiting our freedom of speech and expression.
What one person finds offensive, another person may not.
Therefore, it is impossible to please everyone.
If we were to remove every book, movie, or piece of music that someone found offensive, we would have nothing left.
We would be limiting our access to information and knowledge, which is one of the main purposes of a library.
Lastly, censorship can lead to ignorance and intolerance.
By removing materials from libraries, we are limiting our exposure to different ideas and perspectives.
We are also limiting our ability to learn about different cultures and lifestyles.
This can lead to ignorance and intolerance towards those who are different from us.
In conclusion, censorship is wrong and we should not remove materials from libraries just because some people find them offensive.
Censorship violates our freedom of speech and expression, it is subjective, and it can lead to ignorance and intolerance.
We should respect everyone's right to access information and knowledge, even if we do not agree with them.

The builders of the Empire State Building faced many obstacles while attempting to allow dirigibles to dock there.
All the builders had to start off by making a mooring mast at the top of the building.
They had to make sure it was in the right place so that it wouldn't apply to much pressure to the building.
They also had to make sure it could stand the wind currents.
After all that hard work, Al Smith had a bigger idea.Al Smith wanted to make the mooring mast at the top of the Empire State Building, a place where dirigibles could anchor for several hours.
He also thought that it would be a good place for the dirigles to get fueling if needed and it would be an opportunity for the passengers to get on & off the dirigibles for a break.
Unfortunately for Al Smith, the Plan didn't work.
The builders faced many obstacles when it came to the safety of the dirigibles.
Most dirigibles from outside the United States used hydrogen, which is highly flammable.
The greatest obstacle to the successful use of the mooring mast was nature itself.
The winds on top of the building were constantly shifting due to violent air currents.
Even if the dirigible were tethered to the mooring mast, the back of the ship would swivel around and around the mooring mast.

Dirigibles moored in open landing fields could be weighted down in the back with lead weights, but using these at the Empire State Building, where they would be dangling high above pedestrians on the street, was neither practical nor safe.
Another obstacle was an existing law against airships flying too low over urban areas.
This law would make it illegal for a ship to ever tie up to the building or even approach the area, although two dirigibles did attempt to reach the building before the entire idea was dropped.
In December 1930, the U.S. Navy dirigible Los Angeles approached the mooring mast but could not get close enough to tie up because of forceful winds.

Fearing that the wind would blow the dirigible onto the sharp spires of other buildings in the area, which would puncture the dirigible’s shell, the captain could not even take his hands off the control levers.
